sources.fullCitation: “Gesetz über die Vorführung ausländischer Bildstreifen. Vom 23. Juni 1933.” Reichsgesetzblatt 1933, Teil I, no. 69, issued in Berlin on 27 June 1933, p. 393. Digital page via Wikimedia Commons.
sources.title: Gesetz über die Vorführung ausländischer Bildstreifen, 23 June 1933
sources.creator: Reichsregierung
sources.researchNote: The law of 23 June 1933 extended the 1930 law on the showing of foreign films, as amended in 1932, to 30 June 1936, and empowered the Reich Minister for Popular Enlightenment and Propaganda to issue its implementing ordinances. The ordinance of 28 June 1933 that redefined a German film by citizenship and origin was issued under it and was not printed in the Reichsgesetzblatt; this page shows the law, not the ordinance.

media.title: Reichsgesetzblatt 1933, Teil I, p. 393 — law on the showing of foreign films, 23 June 1933
media.description: The upper part of page 393 of the Reichsgesetzblatt, Teil I, no. 69, issued on 27 June 1933. It prints the law of 23 June 1933 that extended the quota law on foreign films to 1936, signed by Hitler, Goebbels and Frick. The ordinance of 28 June 1933 that redefined a German film by citizenship and origin was issued under this law; it is not printed here.
media.altText: Printed page of the Reichsgesetzblatt 1933 with the masthead and the law on the showing of foreign films of 23 June 1933.
media.publicCaption: Reichsgesetzblatt, 27 June 1933: the law on the showing of foreign films, under which the ordinance of 28 June 1933 redefined a “German film”.
media.publicCreditLine: Reichsgesetzblatt 1933, Teil I, no. 69, p. 393; via Wikimedia Commons.
media.rightsNote: Public domain. Laws published in an official gazette are official works, which German copyright law excludes from protection, so the page was never protected in its source country and the URAA restored nothing.

timelineEvents.title: “German film” redefined by citizenship and origin
timelineEvents.label: 28 June 1933 · “German film” redefined
timelineEvents.shortDescription: An amendment tied the definition of a “German film” to the citizenship and origin of everyone working on it, closing the German market to Kaper and Jurmann.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Two measures turned exclusion into law. The implementing ordinance of 1 July 1932 required that 75 per cent of a film production’s personnel be German, which already told against foreign composers without naming Jews. Its amendment of 28 June 1933 went further and redefined a “German film” by the German citizenship and origin of all those involved in the production. As Jewish citizens of Poland and Austria, Kaper and Jurmann were caught by both conditions at once, and the German market was closed to them.
